title: capacity-contracts-and-soft-isolation-prd-draft
content:
Context
This is a working PRD sketch for a complementary approach to Dedicated capacity: formalizing customer 'capacity contracts' and implementing 'soft isolation' lanes to improve predictability and resource fairness while enabling limited bursts. Unlike previous drafts focused solely on autoscale knobs and credit pools, this explores binding contract semantics + a runtime enforcement model that blends reservation, opportunistic borrowing, and priority-based degradation.

Problem statement
- Customers want predictable tail latency for critical routes while avoiding overpaying for unused reserved GPUs.
- Current reserved pools either feel too rigid (wasted capacity) or too lax (noisy neighbors).
- We need a model that: 1) gives commercial-grade reservation guarantees; 2) allows controlled bursts; 3) enforces isolation without hard cutoffs that break apps.

Goals (measurable)
- Offer three contract classes (Committed, Shared-Guard, Opportunistic) with clear SLOs: throughput, p95 token latency, and burst allowance.
- Keep q95 p95 latency impact from co-tenants under 10% for Committed lanes during normal ops.
- Support per-tenant burst up to 4x baseline for short windows (max 60s) with decay curves applied to avoid sustained overload.
- Provide APIs for customers to configure per-route priority tokens and fallback policies.

Non-goals
- This draft does not propose new physical placement algorithms or introduce new pricing models (pricing will be drafted by GTM).
- Not addressing hardware preemption strategies for spot-like machines here.

High-level approach
1) Capacity contract as first-class object: a contract binds: reserved GPU count (or compute units), contract class, burst budget, and degradation policy. Contracts get enforced by the capacity broker.
2) Soft isolation lanes: runtime maintains logical lanes for Committed and Shared-Guard tenants. Lanes are enforced via admission controls, shaping, and fast-fail fallbacks rather than hard eviction where possible.
3) Burst escrow & decay: each contract accrues a burst escrow (credits) proportional to committed capacity and historical underutilization. Credits are consumed during bursts and decay using an exponential decay curve to prevent credit hoarding.
4) Graceful degradation: when lane limits reached, lower-priority routes are steered to a) queued execution with SLA-aware timeouts, b) lighter quantized model variant, or c) a fallback hosted model.

Design details
- Contract lifecycle: create -> activate (provision warm pool) -> monitor -> readjust (customer ops or autoscale triggers) -> retire.
- Metrics in contract object: reserved_units, active_units, burst_escrow, last_scaled_at, recent_tail_latency (30m), drop_rate. These are surfaced in Console.
- Broker decisions: a request checks contract allowance; if under reserved_units -> immediate; else if burst_escrow > threshold -> allow and deduct with time-decayed charge; else check opportunistic pool (best-effort) -> if not available run fallback.
- Decay model: credits decay with half-life H (configurable per contract class). Example: H=2 hours means credits reduce by 50% every 2h of wall time. This prevents indefinite stacking.
- Prioritization tokens: customers can tag requests with route_priority: critical | standard | low. Broker uses token + contract headroom to decide enforcement and fallback order.

Autoscale interplay
- Autoscaling will be contract-aware: sustained usage above committed units triggers an autoscale recommendation or automated bump (policy-controlled). Contract bumps can be scheduled or immediate depending on customer policy (auto-approve vs. manual).
- To avoid oscillation, autoscaler will require: sustained >70% utilization for T minutes and a burst-adjusted utilization metric that subtracts burst credits consumed.

Isolation enforcement techniques (soft)
- Admission control via token-bucket per-lane + per-tenant allowed concurrency. Token refills respect contract reserves.
- Lightweight shaping: hold short requests (20–200ms) artificially to smooth bursts when opportunistic pool exhausted instead of outright rejecting.
- Per-tenant KV-cache partitioning for large-context models to avoid cross-tenant cache pollution.
- CPU/GPU cgroup soft reservations—enqueue instead of preempt when possible. Use soft limits to maintain node stability.

Operational signals & observability
- Expose contract dashboards: burst_escrow_over_time, credit_decay_curve, lane_misses, fallback_hit_rate, average latency by priority.
- Alerts: lane_miss_rate > X over 5m, burst_escrow depleted for Committed contract, autoscale recommendations pending > Y.

APIs & Console UX
- REST: POST /contracts (specify class, reserved_units, burst_policy, fallback_policy), GET /contracts/:id, PATCH (scale), POST /contracts/:id/claim-burst (simulate).
- Console: interactive graph of escrow build/usage, a slider to demo how much burst remains, and one-click start for temporary bump requests.

Rollout plan (phased)
- Phase 0 (internal): simulate broker with synthetic workload to validate decay and lane behavior.
- Phase 1 (beta): invite 5 customers to opt into Committed and Shared-Guard lanes; monitor real workload patterns and adjust decay half-life.
- Phase 2: automated scaling + public launch for new contracts; add billing hooks.

Open questions / TODOs
- Pricing model alignment: how does burst escrow map to billing? prepaid? metered? (action: GTM input)
- Edge cases: federated tenants across multiple regions—how to enforce global escrow? (infra input needed)
- Fallback experience: define golden path for model selection when falling back (lighter quant, hosted model) — product/ML to propose.
- How to surface legal SLA claims if soft isolation strategies cause visible degradation? (legal + support)

Next steps
- Run capacity-simulator with realistic tenant traces (Sofie + Eng infra)
- Draft API proto and Console mocks (Diego + DX)
- Align with GTM on billing primitives and contract names (pricing workshop)

Notes to reviewers
This is intentionally exploratory: looking for feedback on the contract semantics, decay model, and whether 'soft isolation' is sufficient for enterprise customers who expect strict SLAs. If customers require hard guarantees we should evaluate hybrid model where dedicated physical nodes are pinned to critical contracts.
